title: Brandenburg v. Ohio
short: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) held that the government may not punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it; it overruled Whitney.
trouble: Students leave out one of the elements. All three are needed: intent (directed to), imminence, and likelihood.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

opts.facts: Clarence Brandenburg, a Ku Klux Klan leader in Ohio, invited a television reporter to film a rally. In the film, hooded figures made speeches attacking Black and Jewish Americans and spoke of possible "revengeance" against officials. He was convicted under Ohio's criminal syndicalism law, which punished advocating crime or violence as a means of political reform.
opts.reasoning: The per curiam opinion said the constitutional guarantees of free speech and press do not permit a state to forbid advocacy of the use of force or of law violation "except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or produce such action." Ohio's law punished mere advocacy and assembly, so it fell. Whitney v. California was overruled.

blocks.html: Brandenburg ended the line that began with clear and present danger. Its test has three parts, and all three must be met before advocacy of lawbreaking can be punished.

head: Element
Words in Brandenburg
What it rules out
rows: speech that is careless or reckless about violence but not aimed at it
advocacy of lawbreaking at some later time
"likely to incite or produce such action"
calls to violence that no one is likely to act on

blocks.html: The test protects a great deal of hateful and alarming speech, on purpose. Its defenders say that letting officials punish speech for its tendency to cause harm someday gave them power to silence unpopular causes, from antiwar pamphlets to civil rights groups. In Hess v. Indiana (1973) a protester's remark about taking the street "later" was not punishable because it was not directed to imminent action; in NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware (1982) heated speeches supporting a boycott were protected. Brandenburg does not protect everything: speech that meets all three elements is unprotected incitement, and other categories such as true threats have their own tests.
Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969): government may not punish advocacy of force or lawbreaking unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. It overruled Whitney.

blocks.title: A speech at a rally
blocks.q: At a rally, a speaker says that someday the movement will have to fight its enemies in the streets. Nothing happens. Can the speaker be convicted of incitement?
steps: Likelihood: no sign anyone was about to act.
All three elements are needed; imminence alone fails.
blocks.a: No; the speech is protected under Brandenburg.

blocks.title: A crowd outside a building
blocks.q: A speaker points at a building across the street and tells an angry crowd to break in and burn it right now, and people start toward it. Is that protected?
steps: Intent: the words are directed at producing lawless action.
Imminence: "right now," at a building in view.
Likelihood: the crowd begins to act.
blocks.a: Not protected: it meets all three elements of incitement.

blocks.html: Leaving out one of the elements. All three are needed: intent ("directed to"), imminence and likelihood. A quick check: if any one is missing, Brandenburg protects the speech.
